sentences.en: DistroWatch Weekly, Issue 1190, 14 September 2026 Welcome to this year's 37th issue of DistroWatch Weekly!
Linux distributions are often presented as lightweight, efficient alternatives to commercial operating systems such as Windows.
How small and how efficient can Linux get?
In this week's Questions and Answers column we explore the topic of the world's smallest Linux distributions.
How big was the smallest Linux distribution you have used?
Let us know in the Opinion Poll.
In our News section we talk about Asahi Linux running on M3-powered Apple computers while the FreeBSD project tests a new service manager.
We talk about a new package comparison tool for openSUSE users and share a call for volunteers from the Arch Linux team.
The Linux Mint team have been working on their XApps project, which provides cross-desktop applications for common tasks, and we share highlights below.
Before we dive into those stories we share a look at Vanilla OS 3.
The Vanilla OS distribution provides an immutable, Debian-based operating system with some custom tools.
Jesse Smith took Vanilla OS for a spin and reports on the experience in this week's Feature Story.
Plus we are pleased to share a summary of last week's releases and list the torrents we are seeding.
We wish you all a fantastic week and happy reading!
This week's DistroWatch Weekly is presented by TUXEDO Computers.

Content: Review: Vanilla OS 3 "Reunion" News: Asahi Linux works on M3-powered Apple computers, FreeBSD tests new service manager, Arch seeks help triaging bugs, openSUSE introduces tool to compare package versions, Linux Mint updates XApp, Debian publishes media update Questions and answers: The smallest possible Linux Released last week: FreeBSD 14.5, Spaced Linux 9.26, Ubuntu 24.04.5 Torrent corner: TUXEDO OS, Ubuntu Upcoming releases: Fedora 45 Beta Opinion poll: How small was the smallest Linux you have used?

Reader comments Feature Story (By Jesse Smith) Vanilla OS 3 "Reunion" Vanilla OS, a fixed-release distribution based on Debian (formerly Ubuntu) with the GNOME desktop, is an immutable operating system.
The new Vanilla OS 3 release introduces support for generic ARM (aarch64) machines, adding these devices to its existing support for x86_64 computers.
The release announcement also mentions Vanilla OS 3 ships with GNOME 50 as its only desktop environment which runs Wayland sessions only.

Work has also gone into making reproducible builds: Most images (except NVIDIA images due to kernel modules) are now fully reproducible, meaning the build process always produces bit-for-bit identical images from the same sources.
There have been some changes to the update process too: With so many changes to default apps since Vanilla OS 2 Orchid, we've introduced a new update mode in First Setup.
It runs automatically after an upgrade, allowing you to install new apps and uninstall old ones.
Just a few clicks to confirm the changes, and you're ready to enjoy the latest Vanilla OS experience.
While immutability protects the system, your data is a whole different story.
That's why in Reunion we introduced Vanilla Continuity, a new snapshot-based backup and restore tool that is now part of the image and works together with ABRoot.
It saves your home directories, the list of installed Flatpak apps and ABRoot metadata, then restores them when needed.
I downloaded the x86_64 build of Vanilla which is 1.8GB in size.
I soon found that the distribution runs in UEFI mode only.
Trying to boot in Legacy BIOS mode will start a graphical environment and display a message saying the system will install in UEFI mode only.
Then the system will reboot before it reaches the GNOME desktop.
When running in UEFI mode the distribution launches a graphical environment and displays a welcome window.
We are given the choice of installing Vanilla OS, installing a custom image, running a recovery mode, or powering off the computer.
The system reportedly requires 4GB of RAM and over 50GB of disk space in order to install the distribution, though both of these numbers (as I will point out later in this review) are inflated.
Installing Vanilla uses a custom, graphical system installer.
We are first asked to pick our preferred language from a list, then choose our keyboard from another list, and our timezone from a third list.
We can then select which hard drive to use for storing Vanilla OS.
The distribution offers guided partitioning which will take over an entire disk or manual partitioning.
The manual option offers to launch the GParted application to help us organize the disk.
The installer offers to enable encryption on our partition and, if we accept, it will get us to make up a password to unlock the disk.
The installer copies its files to the drive and then, in my case, it reported success.
The system then reboots.
The first time Vanilla OS boots it launches a first-run welcome wizard.
We are asked to name our computer, make up a username and password combination, and then we are shown a graphical login screen.
The login page has accessibility options for displaying larger text, using an on-screen keyboard, running a screen reader, and displaying fonts in a high contrast.
Once we login we are presented with the GNOME 50 desktop.
Another first-run wizard then launches and offers to enable accessibility options and choose between a light and dark theme (the light theme is selected by default).
The next screen asks us to select the applications we want to run, with the categories labelled Core, Browsers, Common, and Office.
We can click a button next to each category to see which applications it includes.
We can then further customize the selection by toggling specific applications.
For example, clicking on the Browsers category reveals Firefox is selected by default.
However, there are several other options we can choose to install, including Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Floorp, LibreWolf, Zen, Edge, and Vivaldi.
The Office category offers LibreOffice and OnlyOffice.
Once we have made our selections the welcome window displays progress while our new applications are fetched and installed.

Vanilla OS 3 -- Taking the tour (full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Once we have our applications installed the welcome window offers to return us to the GNOME desktop or start a tour, by running GNOME Tour.
The Tour application offers to configure the frequency of update checks.
It also offers to open the software centre so we can install yet more applications.
We're told APX is installed to assist us with development and that the "super key" will display an overview of the desktop.
The Tour then offers to open the settings panel to help us customize the desktop.
There are a few more screens to navigate.
The Tour window will offer to configure cloud accounts and suggests we can visit the Vanilla OS blog to see news updates.
I clicked the blog button and this opened the web browser which had its own five configuration screens to walk through.
For those keeping track at home, this was welcome/configure process number five in my journey.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The application menu (full image size: 298kB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Eventually, I got through all the first-run items and was presented with the GNOME desktop.
GNOME places a thin panel across the top of the screen where we can find the overview button, a clock, and the system tray.
Pressing the super/meta key or clicking the overview button causes a dock to appear at the bottom of the display where we can launch commonly used programs or open a full screen application menu.
Hardware The distribution worked smoothly when I ran it in VirtualBox.
The system integrated well with the virtual environment and I didn't have any problems with Vanilla.
When I ran the distribution on my laptop the experience was also fairly good.
Audio, networking, and keyboard shortcut keys were all detected and worked.
My touchpad translated taps into mouse clicks.
By default the screen was quite dim, set at about 25% brightness, but this could be fixed by using the keyboard shortcut keys.
As I mentioned above, the distribution installs in UEFI mode only.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The GNOME settings panel (full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Measuring disk usage is a bit strange.
Vanilla OS sets up several Btrfs volumes, temporary filesystems, overlays, and containers.
The output from the mount command lists 201 mounted filesystems!
As best as I could tell, Vanilla OS requires about 14GB of disk space when it is first installed, a far cry short of the 50GB the installer demands.
However, with the update images, Btrfs snapshots, and Flatpak bundles Vanilla requires, disk space will be consumed quickly.
When signed into GNOME, Vanilla uses about 1.4GB of RAM.
This is on the heavy side, though it is not unusual for GNOME running a Wayland session.
The distribution does not enable a swap file or partition by default, but it does create a zRAM virtual device in RAM.
This allows the operating system to compress unused memory in a corner of RAM for quick access.
Applications The applications which will be available on Vanilla OS will vary depending on our choices at install time.
We could have virtually no applications, apart from a terminal, file manager, and the GNOME settings panel if we opted for a light setup.

However, mostly sticking with the default options gave me a web browser (Vivaldi, in my case), the GNOME Files file manager, a calendar, clock, weather application, audio player, weather app, and video player.
Both media players worked for me and were able to handle the video and audio files I threw at them.
I decided to install LibreOffice which was available alongside an image viewer, text editor, and resource monitor.
Vanilla ships with manual pages, the GNU command line tools, and the GNU Compiler Collection.
The distribution uses systemd for init and service management functions and runs version 7.1 of the Linux kernel.
The distribution runs the bash shell by default for interactive work and there are virtually no aliases enabled, apart from one to add colour to the output of the ls command.
Software management The desktop software included in Vanilla is mostly supplied by Flatpak bundles, pulled from the Flathub repository.
By default about two dozen of these bundles are installed.
We can fetch additional software using the GNOME Software application.
This software centre uses a three-tab approach.
The first tab allows us to explore available applications and download them.
The second tab shows installed programs and assists us in removing them.
The third tab displays any updates and assists us with installing new versions.
I found GNOME Software worked well for me and without errors.
The interface is pleasantly arranged and fetching new programs requires just a few clicks.
The software centre is a touch slow compared to some other software managers, such as Discover and Linux Mint's equivalent, but I had no problems while using it.

Vanilla OS 3 -- The software centre (full image size: 2.4MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) I'd like to note that each user appears to have their own copy of Flatpak packages, which means each user can have their own version of a program and install or remove applications for their account without affecting the programs available to other users.
I was curious about managing low-level software.
On immutable distributions it is often common to supply portable packages (Flatpak or Snap bundles) as add-ons while keeping the base system fixed.
Other distributions provide some sort of low-level tool for layering on extra packages.
Vanilla OS tries to make adding and managing low-level packages seamless.
When we open a virtual terminal the terminal appears to run inside a container.
This means we can install software in the terminal using Debian's APT package manager and run command line tools.

Since we can access our home directory from inside the container, this makes it seem as though we are installing new programs on Vanilla OS while really we're placing them in an add-on environment and the system is handling the situation transparently.
APX One of the key features of Vanilla OS which gets mentioned on the website and in one of the welcome windows that first greets us, is APX.
The project devotes several documentation pages to APX.
The Getting Started page talks about how to install APX on other distributions.
We don't need this since it is bundled with Vanilla OS.
The Introduction page gives a quick overview of APX: "APX is a versatile command-line interface (CLI) tool designed to simplify the management of operating system containers.
With a focus on efficiency and user-friendliness, APX empowers users to create, manage, and customize containers for a variety of applications and services."
This is a decent big-picture description, but I still wasn't sure what APX actually does in practical terms.
There is another page for working with package managers which tells us how to teach APX about package managers it might not already know.
Apparently APX knows something about how certain popular package managers work.
However, the documentation doesn't explain what to do with this information once we teach APX or what to do with the package manager information already baked into the application.
There is yet another page about working with types of containers, but again no practical information about what APX does in these situations or why we would use it.
There are no practical, hands on examples or goals mentioned.
The package managers APX knows about (dnf, apk, pacman, etc) are not on the system.
I thought maybe APX could be used to manage these package managers inside containers.
However, after reading five sections of the handbook and browsing the APX built-in help screens I could not find any examples of this or how APX is meant to be used.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The graphical APX utility (full image size: 2.0MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) There is a graphical tool for APX.
I launched it and found it just provides the same list of supported package managers and containers as the command line tool.
Using the graphical interface I could not find any hints as to what it was meant to be used for or why it is considered a key component of Vanilla OS.
All of this is to say that APX might be useful and it might be interesting, but I could not find any information about why people would use it or practical steps for doing so.
The documentation throws around buzzwords, such as "simplify" and "efficiency", but not what is being simplified or how or why people would benefit from using it.
Other observations At one point during my trial I created a second user account.
With this new account I could sign into GNOME and the system ran me through the same welcome experience, asking me to select which applications I wanted.
(Each user has their own set of Flatpak bundles.)
For the most part, running this second user account worked and I could fetch and run applications.
The exception was the virtual terminal.
When the second user tried to open a terminal window a message would appear indicating it was setting up a container.
Then a brief message would appear saying setting up the environment failed and the terminal window would close.
This feels like an odd limitation or oversight: not allowing any users apart from the first one run a terminal window.
It makes me wonder if anyone on the Vanilla team has tried running a system with more than one user.

Vanilla OS 3 -- Running the command line APX tool (full image size: 2.9MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Conclusions What I found intriguing, and sometimes frustrating, during my trial with Vanilla OS was that the distribution seems to be implementing some interesting concepts - even some complex and technically challenging concepts - and mostly doing it well, but none of it benefited me as a user.
The distribution adds the complexity of immutability, but that's not helpful for me, that's something I need to work around.
It's not as though the system being immutable is going to make the Debian base, of all things, more stable.
Instead all it does is gum up the works when I try to run a terminal as the second user.
The website and documentation talk a bit about APX, but none of it is useful information or provides any hint as to how it will make my computing experience better.

In a similar vein, I went through five welcome screens and first-run configuration guides which, I'm sure, could be helpful for beginners, but it just meant I spent an extra five or ten minutes setting up my system.
Since Vanilla isn't targeting beginners (their focus is on developer tools and containers) gearing their welcoming processes toward newcomers feels off brand.
Ultimately, Vanilla OS experiments with some technologies well, it makes running Debian with a layer of containers work (mostly) smoothly.
As a proof of concept, it's a solid demonstration.
Vanilla does a good job of layering tools like Flatpak on top of a Debian base.
The question I kept asking myself throughout my trial though was: how does this help me use my computer?
For me, the complexities added by Vanilla just impeded what I was doing, in ways Debian would not.
Vanilla is heavier, it is more complex, it layers tools like Btrfs, zRAM, and Flatpaks which use up more resources.
Vanilla sets up more mount points, runs more wizards, includes more container technology.
All of this is interesting, but it doesn't make my computing experience or development processes faster or smoother or better in any practical way that I can find.

Mostly, it made me want to switch to running the distribution's parent, Debian, to get the same underlying benefits without the extra layers and resource consumption. * * * * * Hardware used in this review My physical test equipment for this review was an HP DY2048CA laptop with the following specifications: Processor: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz Display: Intel integrated video Storage: Western Digital 512GB solid state drive Memory: 8GB of RAM Wireless network device: Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX201 + BT Wireless network card * * * * * Visitor supplied rating Vanilla OS has a visitor supplied average rating of: 6.5/10 from 37 review(s).
Have you used Vanilla OS?
You can leave your own review of the project on our ratings page.

Miscellaneous News (by Jesse Smith) Asahi Linux works on M3-powered Apple computers, FreeBSD tests new service manager, Arch seeks help triaging bugs, openSUSE introduces tool to compare package versions, Linux Mint updates XApp, Debian publishes media update The Asahi Linux project has published good news for people running Apple's M-series hardware.

The Asahi project now supports installing Linux on M3-powered devices: "It's been a while since we did a blog post outside of the progress reports, and today's as good an occasion for one as any; support for M3 series machines has now been merged into the installer.
In other words, Asahi Linux now officially supports Macs with an M3 series SoC!
Linux support for M3 series SoCs and the machines powered by them is now in a state where almost everything supported on the M1 and M2 series machines just works.
This includes the webcam, internal microphones, USB (up to the hardware limit of USB 3 10Gb/s), hardware accelerated video decoding including support for AV1, WiFi, Bluetooth, and much more!
The only major exceptions remain full DCP support and the GPU, which we will have more news on in the coming months.
Do not expect performant or power-efficient 3D acceleration right now."

Details on how to test M3 support, along with a list of limitations, are provided in the project's announcement. * * * * * Over the years there have been a number of discussions in the FreeBSD community regarding service management and possible alternatives to the current rc tools for launching services.
Some alternatives have been tested over the years, including running OpenRC in the GhostBSD desktop offshoot of FreeBSD.
Baptiste Daroussin has another option which is ready to test.
The new tool, called rcd, imports a lot of the beneficial ideas from systemd while avoiding the pain points systemd has inflicted.
"rcd(8) is a service manager daemon called by init(8) (in place of /etc/rc).
It reads service definitions from UCL unit files (/etc/rcd.d/*.ucl), builds a dependency DAG, and starts services in parallel.
After boot completes, it forks to background and stays running as a supervision daemon (automatically restarting failed services and accepting control commands via a UNIX socket)."

The post from Daroussin goes on to share information on how to install and run rcd, list key features, and the message points out rcd is 100% compatible with the existing rc service manager, making switching between the two seamless. * * * * * Frederik Schwan of the Arch Linux project has put out a call for volunteers to help Arch deal with bug reports.
Many projects have seen a surge in bug tickets in recent months, due to LLM-created reports, and Arch is hoping to get help triaging bugs submitted to their GitLab account.
"We are searching for additional helping hands on our GitLab.
Offering sources for thousands of packages requires triaging (and sometimes closing) the many issues that users report over time.

As a bug wrangler you would be helping the distribution with triaging tickets across all package source repositories and assigning them to relevant package maintainers, as well as closing invalid ones and/or investigating the topics at hand (if applicable)."

The post includes contact information where people can reach out to volunteer. * * * * * If you have ever wanted to compare the package versions between openSUSE's Leap and Tumbleweed branches and didn't want to manually compare the versions yourself, we have the DistroWatch package comparison page.
This page will display the upstream stable version of a package as well as provide the package versions for any two distributions, or any two versions of a distribution.
Now, alternatively, the openSUSE project provides its own implementation of this feature to compare packages between openSUSE Leap and openSUSE Tumbleweed.

"The tool pulls the archive indexes straight from download.opensuse.org; this is for open-source software (oss) and non-oss, x86_64 and noarch and it's done for Tumbleweed, Leap 16.1, and Leap 16.0; then it compares the upstream version of every source package it finds.
The result is a single sortable, filterable table with a timestamp on it."

The new osdiff tool is now live and provides a filter for narrowing down the list of compared packages. * * * * * The Linux Mint project maintains a collection of applications, called XApp, which are desktop-neutral forks of GNOME applications.
The XApps now have their own website to make it easier to discover and learn about the applications.
"The XApp project started within Linux Mint but it has grown a lot since then.
Its libraries, tools and applications are used in many desktops and distributions.
It was given a new website to make it easier to discover all its components.
Thingy, known as the 'Library' in the desktop, was redesigned.
Until now, documents were grouped by application.
For instance, PDF files and all the other document types supported by XReader were grouped together under 'Document Viewer'.
The library now organizes documents by type instead.
It no longer matters which applications are installed or which formats they support."
Further information is provided in the Linux Mint monthly newsletter. * * * * * The Debian project has published updated install media for Debian 13 "Trixie".
"The Debian project is pleased to announce the seventh update of its stable distribution Debian 13 (codename Trixie).
This point release mainly adds corrections for security issues, along with a few adjustments for serious problems.
Security advisories have already been published separately and are referenced where available.
Please note that the point release does not constitute a new version of Debian 13 but only updates some of the packages included.
There is no need to throw away old Trixie media.
After installation, packages can be upgraded to the current versions using an up-to-date Debian mirror." * * * * * These and other news stories can be found on our Headlines page.

Questions and Answers (by Jesse Smith) The smallest possible Linux Honey-I-shrank-the-distro asks: Some people say Linux is smaller and lighter than other operating systems, but how small can Linux get compared to others?
DistroWatch answers: For the sake of comparison, Microsoft says the minimal system requirements for Windows 11 are: a dual-core, 64-bit x86_64 processor, 4GB of RAM, and 64GB of storage.
Even the heavier Linux distributions require about half those resources to perform a full install and then run a desktop and a web browser.
Linux distributions can get really small!
The smallest Linux distribution I've run on my own machines was about 1.4MB in size (that's megabytes, not gigabytes).
It was called Tom's Root Boot and ran from a 3.5-inch floppy disk.
It was quite minimal.
It included the Linux kernel with minimal features enabled and a handful of command line tools only.
It could be used for basic system rescue operations.
Granted, that was about 20 years ago and modern versions of the Linux kernel are a bit too big to run from a floppy disk.
In recent memory, one of the smallest Linux distributions I have tried was Minimal Linux Live, which was about a 7MB download.
That's just enough for the kernel, a shell, and a few userland utilities, again mostly for system rescue purposes.
There are a few other distributions which are in the same range.
Tiny Core's most compact edition is about 17MB and SliTaz has an edition which is under 50MB.
These distributions are probably as small as you will be able to get, realistically, and still have an operating system which can boot on a personal computer.
There are some smaller, embedded Linux distributions that are not meant for use by the general public.
Linux can power all sorts of small devices and I've heard of people booting a Linux kernel on anything from home appliances to vape pens.
Whenever we talk about how small Linux can get or how few resources it can be made to consume, I think it is important to include context.
Specifically, what do we want to accomplish with this miniature distribution?
We can distill the Linux kernel and userland down to a few megabytes, but it won't be useful for many things.
As soon as we start to add functionality, the size will need to creep upward.
If we want a command line experience, we will need at least 10MB of disk space and around 25MB of RAM, if we want to add a graphical environment then the requirements go upward.
Tiny Core Linux manages to provide a desktop and package manager with about 24MB of disk space and a little under 100MB of RAM.
This is probably as small as we can get and provide any degree of practical personal computing.
In short, on the heavier end, big Linux distros can get by with about half the resources of Windows 11.

On the lighter end, there are some Linux distributions which can run a small desktop and a few applications with about 1% of the resources Microsoft says Windows 11 requires. * * * * * Additional answers can be found in our Questions and Answers archive.
Released Last Week FreeBSD 14.5 The FreeBSD project has published an update to FreeBSD's 14.x series.
The new version, 14.5, provides several fixes and introduces some changes to the userland utilities.
"The rc.firewall script now supports reading IP addresses or subnets from on-disk files for the firewall_allowservices and firewall_trusted list variables.
Elements that look like absolute paths are read line by line, skipping comments and blank lines, and the first word on each line is treated as an address or subnet.
The default history size in sh(1) has been increased from 100 to 128, complying with the POSIX.1-2024 minimum requirement.
LTO-10 and LTO-10P density codes and cartridge specifications have been added to mt(1) and libmt, enabling detection and reporting of the new tape formats.
The default behaviour of pwd(1) has changed from -P to -L, aligning with POSIX semantics.
The ipfw(8) binary now includes a fallback mechanism to support the new kernel interface introduced in FreeBSD 15.0.
When running with a 15.0+ kernel, ipfw(8) automatically invokes a bundled ipfw15 binary to load firewall rules, ensuring compatibility during upgrade procedures.
The daemon(8) utility now supports the -m option to specify the output file mode, allowing non-root log collectors to access log files."
Additional information can be found in the release announcement and in the release notes.
Spaced Linux 9.26 Spaced Linux 9.26 has been released.
Spaced Linux is a desktop Linux distribution based on Devuan's "Unstable" branch and featuring the MATE desktop environment with the Compiz compositing window manager.

"Spaced Linux 9.26 is a major production release focused on upgrade reliability, graphics-driver recovery, desktop startup resilience, signed package delivery, and substantially stronger automated release validation.

System updates and upgrade reliability: reworked Spaced Update to handle complete operating system upgrades more safely and predictably; added a dedicated APT transaction guard so package changes are protected during the actual locked package-management operation rather than only during preliminary checks; improved handling of package refreshes, native package upgrades, Flatpak updates, release-marker changes, and error reporting; added explicit testing for upgrades from earlier Spaced Linux installations to reduce the chance of regressions affecting existing users; added package-payload validation to confirm that the packages delivered by the production repository match the expected release; added release-identity checks so the built ISO, installed release metadata, package repository, and release version cannot silently drift apart...."
Continue to the detailed release notes for further information.

The new update, version 24.04.5, introduces fixes and improvements: "Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, code-named 'Noble Numbat', is here.
The team has been hard at work through this cycle, together with the community and our partners, to introduce new features and fix bugs.
As usual, this point release includes many updates and updated installation media has been provided, so that fewer updates will need to be downloaded after installation.
These include security updates and corrections for other high-severity bugs, with a focus on maintaining stability and compatibility with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS."

Welcome to this year's 37th issue of DistroWatch Weekly! Linux distributions are often presented as lightweight, efficient alternatives to commercial operating systems such as Windows. How small and how efficient can Linux get? In this week's Questions and Answers column we explore the topic of the world's smallest Linux distributions. How big was the smallest Linux distribution you have used? Let us know in the Opinion Poll. In our News section we talk about Asahi Linux running on M3-powered Apple computers while the FreeBSD project tests a new service manager. We talk about a new package comparison tool for openSUSE users and share a call for volunteers from the Arch Linux team. The Linux Mint team have been working on their XApps project, which provides cross-desktop applications for common tasks, and we share highlights below. Before we dive into those stories we share a look at Vanilla OS 3. The Vanilla OS distribution provides an immutable, Debian-based operating system with some custom tools. Jesse Smith took Vanilla OS for a spin and reports on the experience in this week's Feature Story. Plus we are pleased to share a summary of last week's releases and list the torrents we are seeding. We wish you all a fantastic week and happy reading!

blocks.html_en: Feature Story (By Jesse Smith)

sentences.en: Feature Story (By Jesse Smith)

blocks.html_en:
Vanilla OS 3 "Reunion" Vanilla OS, a fixed-release distribution based on Debian (formerly Ubuntu) with the GNOME desktop, is an immutable operating system. The new Vanilla OS 3 release introduces support for generic ARM (aarch64) machines, adding these devices to its existing support for x86_64 computers. The release announcement also mentions Vanilla OS 3 ships with GNOME 50 as its only desktop environment which runs Wayland sessions only. Work has also gone into making reproducible builds:
Most images (except NVIDIA images due to kernel modules) are now fully reproducible, meaning the build process always produces bit-for-bit identical images from the same sources.
There have been some changes to the update process too:
With so many changes to default apps since Vanilla OS 2 Orchid, we've introduced a new update mode in First Setup. It runs automatically after an upgrade, allowing you to install new apps and uninstall old ones. Just a few clicks to confirm the changes, and you're ready to enjoy the latest Vanilla OS experience.

While immutability protects the system, your data is a whole different story. That's why in Reunion we introduced Vanilla Continuity, a new snapshot-based backup and restore tool that is now part of the image and works together with ABRoot. It saves your home directories, the list of installed Flatpak apps and ABRoot metadata, then restores them when needed.

I downloaded the x86_64 build of Vanilla which is 1.8GB in size. I soon found that the distribution runs in UEFI mode only. Trying to boot in Legacy BIOS mode will start a graphical environment and display a message saying the system will install in UEFI mode only. Then the system will reboot before it reaches the GNOME desktop.

When running in UEFI mode the distribution launches a graphical environment and displays a welcome window. We are given the choice of installing Vanilla OS, installing a custom image, running a recovery mode, or powering off the computer. The system reportedly requires 4GB of RAM and over 50GB of disk space in order to install the distribution, though both of these numbers (as I will point out later in this review) are inflated.

Installing

Vanilla uses a custom, graphical system installer. We are first asked to pick our preferred language from a list, then choose our keyboard from another list, and our timezone from a third list. We can then select which hard drive to use for storing Vanilla OS. The distribution offers guided partitioning which will take over an entire disk or manual partitioning. The manual option offers to launch the GParted application to help us organize the disk.

The installer offers to enable encryption on our partition and, if we accept, it will get us to make up a password to unlock the disk. The installer copies its files to the drive and then, in my case, it reported success. The system then reboots.

The first time Vanilla OS boots it launches a first-run welcome wizard. We are asked to name our computer, make up a username and password combination, and then we are shown a graphical login screen. The login page has accessibility options for displaying larger text, using an on-screen keyboard, running a screen reader, and displaying fonts in a high contrast.

Once we login we are presented with the GNOME 50 desktop. Another first-run wizard then launches and offers to enable accessibility options and choose between a light and dark theme (the light theme is selected by default). The next screen asks us to select the applications we want to run, with the categories labelled Core, Browsers, Common, and Office. We can click a button next to each category to see which applications it includes. We can then further customize the selection by toggling specific applications. For example, clicking on the Browsers category reveals Firefox is selected by default. However, there are several other options we can choose to install, including Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Floorp, LibreWolf, Zen, Edge, and Vivaldi. The Office category offers LibreOffice and OnlyOffice. Once we have made our selections the welcome window displays progress while our new applications are fetched and installed.


Vanilla OS 3 -- Taking the tour
(full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


Once we have our applications installed the welcome window offers to return us to the GNOME desktop or start a tour, by running GNOME Tour. The Tour application offers to configure the frequency of update checks. It also offers to open the software centre so we can install yet more applications. We're told APX is installed to assist us with development and that the "super key" will display an overview of the desktop. The Tour then offers to open the settings panel to help us customize the desktop.

There are a few more screens to navigate. The Tour window will offer to configure cloud accounts and suggests we can visit the Vanilla OS blog to see news updates. I clicked the blog button and this opened the web browser which had its own five configuration screens to walk through. For those keeping track at home, this was welcome/configure process number five in my journey.


Vanilla OS 3 -- The application menu
(full image size: 298kB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


Eventually, I got through all the first-run items and was presented with the GNOME desktop. GNOME places a thin panel across the top of the screen where we can find the overview button, a clock, and the system tray. Pressing the super/meta key or clicking the overview button causes a dock to appear at the bottom of the display where we can launch commonly used programs or open a full screen application menu.

Hardware

The distribution worked smoothly when I ran it in VirtualBox. The system integrated well with the virtual environment and I didn't have any problems with Vanilla. When I ran the distribution on my laptop the experience was also fairly good. Audio, networking, and keyboard shortcut keys were all detected and worked. My touchpad translated taps into mouse clicks. By default the screen was quite dim, set at about 25% brightness, but this could be fixed by using the keyboard shortcut keys. As I mentioned above, the distribution installs in UEFI mode only.


Vanilla OS 3 -- The GNOME settings panel
(full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


Measuring disk usage is a bit strange. Vanilla OS sets up several Btrfs volumes, temporary filesystems, overlays, and containers. The output from the mount command lists 201 mounted filesystems! As best as I could tell, Vanilla OS requires about 14GB of disk space when it is first installed, a far cry short of the 50GB the installer demands. However, with the update images, Btrfs snapshots, and Flatpak bundles Vanilla requires, disk space will be consumed quickly.

When signed into GNOME, Vanilla uses about 1.4GB of RAM. This is on the heavy side, though it is not unusual for GNOME running a Wayland session. The distribution does not enable a swap file or partition by default, but it does create a zRAM virtual device in RAM. This allows the operating system to compress unused memory in a corner of RAM for quick access.

Applications

The applications which will be available on Vanilla OS will vary depending on our choices at install time. We could have virtually no applications, apart from a terminal, file manager, and the GNOME settings panel if we opted for a light setup. However, mostly sticking with the default options gave me a web browser (Vivaldi, in my case), the GNOME Files file manager, a calendar, clock, weather application, audio player, weather app, and video player. Both media players worked for me and were able to handle the video and audio files I threw at them. I decided to install LibreOffice which was available alongside an image viewer, text editor, and resource monitor.

Vanilla ships with manual pages, the GNU command line tools, and the GNU Compiler Collection. The distribution uses systemd for init and service management functions and runs version 7.1 of the Linux kernel.

The distribution runs the bash shell by default for interactive work and there are virtually no aliases enabled, apart from one to add colour to the output of the ls command.

Software management

The desktop software included in Vanilla is mostly supplied by Flatpak bundles, pulled from the Flathub repository. By default about two dozen of these bundles are installed. We can fetch additional software using the GNOME Software application. This software centre uses a three-tab approach. The first tab allows us to explore available applications and download them. The second tab shows installed programs and assists us in removing them. The third tab displays any updates and assists us with installing new versions.

I found GNOME Software worked well for me and without errors. The interface is pleasantly arranged and fetching new programs requires just a few clicks. The software centre is a touch slow compared to some other software managers, such as Discover and Linux Mint's equivalent, but I had no problems while using it.


Vanilla OS 3 -- The software centre
(full image size: 2.4MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


I'd like to note that each user appears to have their own copy of Flatpak packages, which means each user can have their own version of a program and install or remove applications for their account without affecting the programs available to other users.

I was curious about managing low-level software. On immutable distributions it is often common to supply portable packages (Flatpak or Snap bundles) as add-ons while keeping the base system fixed. Other distributions provide some sort of low-level tool for layering on extra packages. Vanilla OS tries to make adding and managing low-level packages seamless. When we open a virtual terminal the terminal appears to run inside a container. This means we can install software in the terminal using Debian's APT package manager and run command line tools. Since we can access our home directory from inside the container, this makes it seem as though we are installing new programs on Vanilla OS while really we're placing them in an add-on environment and the system is handling the situation transparently.

APX

One of the key features of Vanilla OS which gets mentioned on the website and in one of the welcome windows that first greets us, is APX. The project devotes several documentation pages to APX. The Getting Started page talks about how to install APX on other distributions. We don't need this since it is bundled with Vanilla OS.

The Introduction page gives a quick overview of APX: "APX is a versatile command-line interface (CLI) tool designed to simplify the management of operating system containers. With a focus on efficiency and user-friendliness, APX empowers users to create, manage, and customize containers for a variety of applications and services." This is a decent big-picture description, but I still wasn't sure what APX actually does in practical terms.

There is another page for working with package managers which tells us how to teach APX about package managers it might not already know. Apparently APX knows something about how certain popular package managers work. However, the documentation doesn't explain what to do with this information once we teach APX or what to do with the package manager information already baked into the application. There is yet another page about working with types of containers, but again no practical information about what APX does in these situations or why we would use it. There are no practical, hands on examples or goals mentioned.

The package managers APX knows about (dnf, apk, pacman, etc) are not on the system. I thought maybe APX could be used to manage these package managers inside containers. However, after reading five sections of the handbook and browsing the APX built-in help screens I could not find any examples of this or how APX is meant to be used.


Vanilla OS 3 -- The graphical APX utility
(full image size: 2.0MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


There is a graphical tool for APX. I launched it and found it just provides the same list of supported package managers and containers as the command line tool. Using the graphical interface I could not find any hints as to what it was meant to be used for or why it is considered a key component of Vanilla OS. All of this is to say that APX might be useful and it might be interesting, but I could not find any information about why people would use it or practical steps for doing so. The documentation throws around buzzwords, such as "simplify" and "efficiency", but not what is being simplified or how or why people would benefit from using it.

Other observations

At one point during my trial I created a second user account. With this new account I could sign into GNOME and the system ran me through the same welcome experience, asking me to select which applications I wanted. (Each user has their own set of Flatpak bundles.) For the most part, running this second user account worked and I could fetch and run applications. The exception was the virtual terminal. When the second user tried to open a terminal window a message would appear indicating it was setting up a container. Then a brief message would appear saying setting up the environment failed and the terminal window would close.

This feels like an odd limitation or oversight: not allowing any users apart from the first one run a terminal window. It makes me wonder if anyone on the Vanilla team has tried running a system with more than one user.


Vanilla OS 3 -- Running the command line APX tool
(full image size: 2.9MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels)


Conclusions

What I found intriguing, and sometimes frustrating, during my trial with Vanilla OS was that the distribution seems to be implementing some interesting concepts - even some complex and technically challenging concepts - and mostly doing it well, but none of it benefited me as a user. The distribution adds the complexity of immutability, but that's not helpful for me, that's something I need to work around. It's not as though the system being immutable is going to make the Debian base, of all things, more stable. Instead all it does is gum up the works when I try to run a terminal as the second user.

The website and documentation talk a bit about APX, but none of it is useful information or provides any hint as to how it will make my computing experience better. In a similar vein, I went through five welcome screens and first-run configuration guides which, I'm sure, could be helpful for beginners, but it just meant I spent an extra five or ten minutes setting up my system. Since Vanilla isn't targeting beginners (their focus is on developer tools and containers) gearing their welcoming processes toward newcomers feels off brand.

Ultimately, Vanilla OS experiments with some technologies well, it makes running Debian with a layer of containers work (mostly) smoothly. As a proof of concept, it's a solid demonstration. Vanilla does a good job of layering tools like Flatpak on top of a Debian base. The question I kept asking myself throughout my trial though was: how does this help me use my computer? For me, the complexities added by Vanilla just impeded what I was doing, in ways Debian would not. Vanilla is heavier, it is more complex, it layers tools like Btrfs, zRAM, and Flatpaks which use up more resources. Vanilla sets up more mount points, runs more wizards, includes more container technology. All of this is interesting, but it doesn't make my computing experience or development processes faster or smoother or better in any practical way that I can find. Mostly, it made me want to switch to running the distribution's parent, Debian, to get the same underlying benefits without the extra layers and resource consumption.

* * * * *

Hardware used in this review

My physical test equipment for this review was an HP DY2048CA laptop with the following specifications:

  • Processor: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz
  • Display: Intel integrated video
  • Storage: Western Digital 512GB solid state drive
  • Memory: 8GB of RAM
  • Wireless network device: Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX201 + BT Wireless network card

* * * * *

Visitor supplied rating

Vanilla OS has a visitor supplied average rating of: 6.5/10 from 37 review(s).
Have you used Vanilla OS? You can leave your own review of the project on our ratings page.

Once we have made our selections the welcome window displays progress while our new applications are fetched and installed.

Vanilla OS 3 -- Taking the tour (full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Once we have our applications installed the welcome window offers to return us to the GNOME desktop or start a tour, by running GNOME Tour.
The Tour application offers to configure the frequency of update checks.
It also offers to open the software centre so we can install yet more applications.
We're told APX is installed to assist us with development and that the "super key" will display an overview of the desktop.
The Tour then offers to open the settings panel to help us customize the desktop.
There are a few more screens to navigate.
The Tour window will offer to configure cloud accounts and suggests we can visit the Vanilla OS blog to see news updates.
I clicked the blog button and this opened the web browser which had its own five configuration screens to walk through.
For those keeping track at home, this was welcome/configure process number five in my journey.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The application menu (full image size: 298kB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Eventually, I got through all the first-run items and was presented with the GNOME desktop.
GNOME places a thin panel across the top of the screen where we can find the overview button, a clock, and the system tray.
Pressing the super/meta key or clicking the overview button causes a dock to appear at the bottom of the display where we can launch commonly used programs or open a full screen application menu.
Hardware The distribution worked smoothly when I ran it in VirtualBox.
The system integrated well with the virtual environment and I didn't have any problems with Vanilla.
When I ran the distribution on my laptop the experience was also fairly good.
Audio, networking, and keyboard shortcut keys were all detected and worked.
My touchpad translated taps into mouse clicks.
By default the screen was quite dim, set at about 25% brightness, but this could be fixed by using the keyboard shortcut keys.
As I mentioned above, the distribution installs in UEFI mode only.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The GNOME settings panel (full image size: 2.5MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Measuring disk usage is a bit strange.
Vanilla OS sets up several Btrfs volumes, temporary filesystems, overlays, and containers.
The output from the mount command lists 201 mounted filesystems!
As best as I could tell, Vanilla OS requires about 14GB of disk space when it is first installed, a far cry short of the 50GB the installer demands.
However, with the update images, Btrfs snapshots, and Flatpak bundles Vanilla requires, disk space will be consumed quickly.
When signed into GNOME, Vanilla uses about 1.4GB of RAM.
This is on the heavy side, though it is not unusual for GNOME running a Wayland session.
The distribution does not enable a swap file or partition by default, but it does create a zRAM virtual device in RAM.
This allows the operating system to compress unused memory in a corner of RAM for quick access.
Applications The applications which will be available on Vanilla OS will vary depending on our choices at install time.
We could have virtually no applications, apart from a terminal, file manager, and the GNOME settings panel if we opted for a light setup.

However, mostly sticking with the default options gave me a web browser (Vivaldi, in my case), the GNOME Files file manager, a calendar, clock, weather application, audio player, weather app, and video player.
Both media players worked for me and were able to handle the video and audio files I threw at them.
I decided to install LibreOffice which was available alongside an image viewer, text editor, and resource monitor.
Vanilla ships with manual pages, the GNU command line tools, and the GNU Compiler Collection.
The distribution uses systemd for init and service management functions and runs version 7.1 of the Linux kernel.
The distribution runs the bash shell by default for interactive work and there are virtually no aliases enabled, apart from one to add colour to the output of the ls command.
Software management The desktop software included in Vanilla is mostly supplied by Flatpak bundles, pulled from the Flathub repository.
By default about two dozen of these bundles are installed.
We can fetch additional software using the GNOME Software application.
This software centre uses a three-tab approach.
The first tab allows us to explore available applications and download them.
The second tab shows installed programs and assists us in removing them.
The third tab displays any updates and assists us with installing new versions.
I found GNOME Software worked well for me and without errors.
The interface is pleasantly arranged and fetching new programs requires just a few clicks.
The software centre is a touch slow compared to some other software managers, such as Discover and Linux Mint's equivalent, but I had no problems while using it.

Vanilla OS 3 -- The software centre (full image size: 2.4MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) I'd like to note that each user appears to have their own copy of Flatpak packages, which means each user can have their own version of a program and install or remove applications for their account without affecting the programs available to other users.
I was curious about managing low-level software.
On immutable distributions it is often common to supply portable packages (Flatpak or Snap bundles) as add-ons while keeping the base system fixed.
Other distributions provide some sort of low-level tool for layering on extra packages.
Vanilla OS tries to make adding and managing low-level packages seamless.
When we open a virtual terminal the terminal appears to run inside a container.
This means we can install software in the terminal using Debian's APT package manager and run command line tools.

Since we can access our home directory from inside the container, this makes it seem as though we are installing new programs on Vanilla OS while really we're placing them in an add-on environment and the system is handling the situation transparently.
APX One of the key features of Vanilla OS which gets mentioned on the website and in one of the welcome windows that first greets us, is APX.
The project devotes several documentation pages to APX.
The Getting Started page talks about how to install APX on other distributions.
We don't need this since it is bundled with Vanilla OS.
The Introduction page gives a quick overview of APX: "APX is a versatile command-line interface (CLI) tool designed to simplify the management of operating system containers.
With a focus on efficiency and user-friendliness, APX empowers users to create, manage, and customize containers for a variety of applications and services."
This is a decent big-picture description, but I still wasn't sure what APX actually does in practical terms.
There is another page for working with package managers which tells us how to teach APX about package managers it might not already know.
Apparently APX knows something about how certain popular package managers work.
However, the documentation doesn't explain what to do with this information once we teach APX or what to do with the package manager information already baked into the application.
There is yet another page about working with types of containers, but again no practical information about what APX does in these situations or why we would use it.
There are no practical, hands on examples or goals mentioned.
The package managers APX knows about (dnf, apk, pacman, etc) are not on the system.
I thought maybe APX could be used to manage these package managers inside containers.
However, after reading five sections of the handbook and browsing the APX built-in help screens I could not find any examples of this or how APX is meant to be used.
Vanilla OS 3 -- The graphical APX utility (full image size: 2.0MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) There is a graphical tool for APX.
I launched it and found it just provides the same list of supported package managers and containers as the command line tool.
Using the graphical interface I could not find any hints as to what it was meant to be used for or why it is considered a key component of Vanilla OS.
All of this is to say that APX might be useful and it might be interesting, but I could not find any information about why people would use it or practical steps for doing so.
The documentation throws around buzzwords, such as "simplify" and "efficiency", but not what is being simplified or how or why people would benefit from using it.
Other observations At one point during my trial I created a second user account.
With this new account I could sign into GNOME and the system ran me through the same welcome experience, asking me to select which applications I wanted.
(Each user has their own set of Flatpak bundles.)
For the most part, running this second user account worked and I could fetch and run applications.
The exception was the virtual terminal.
When the second user tried to open a terminal window a message would appear indicating it was setting up a container.
Then a brief message would appear saying setting up the environment failed and the terminal window would close.
This feels like an odd limitation or oversight: not allowing any users apart from the first one run a terminal window.
It makes me wonder if anyone on the Vanilla team has tried running a system with more than one user.

Vanilla OS 3 -- Running the command line APX tool (full image size: 2.9MB, resolution: 1920x1080 pixels) Conclusions What I found intriguing, and sometimes frustrating, during my trial with Vanilla OS was that the distribution seems to be implementing some interesting concepts - even some complex and technically challenging concepts - and mostly doing it well, but none of it benefited me as a user.
The distribution adds the complexity of immutability, but that's not helpful for me, that's something I need to work around.
It's not as though the system being immutable is going to make the Debian base, of all things, more stable.
Instead all it does is gum up the works when I try to run a terminal as the second user.
The website and documentation talk a bit about APX, but none of it is useful information or provides any hint as to how it will make my computing experience better.

In a similar vein, I went through five welcome screens and first-run configuration guides which, I'm sure, could be helpful for beginners, but it just meant I spent an extra five or ten minutes setting up my system.
Since Vanilla isn't targeting beginners (their focus is on developer tools and containers) gearing their welcoming processes toward newcomers feels off brand.
Ultimately, Vanilla OS experiments with some technologies well, it makes running Debian with a layer of containers work (mostly) smoothly.
As a proof of concept, it's a solid demonstration.
Vanilla does a good job of layering tools like Flatpak on top of a Debian base.
The question I kept asking myself throughout my trial though was: how does this help me use my computer?
For me, the complexities added by Vanilla just impeded what I was doing, in ways Debian would not.
Vanilla is heavier, it is more complex, it layers tools like Btrfs, zRAM, and Flatpaks which use up more resources.
Vanilla sets up more mount points, runs more wizards, includes more container technology.
All of this is interesting, but it doesn't make my computing experience or development processes faster or smoother or better in any practical way that I can find.

Mostly, it made me want to switch to running the distribution's parent, Debian, to get the same underlying benefits without the extra layers and resource consumption. * * * * * Hardware used in this review My physical test equipment for this review was an HP DY2048CA laptop with the following specifications: Processor: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-1135G7 @ 2.40GHz Display: Intel integrated video Storage: Western Digital 512GB solid state drive Memory: 8GB of RAM Wireless network device: Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX201 + BT Wireless network card * * * * * Visitor supplied rating Vanilla OS has a visitor supplied average rating of: 6.5/10 from 37 review(s).

With so many changes to default apps since Vanilla OS 2 Orchid, we've introduced a new update mode in First Setup. It runs automatically after an upgrade, allowing you to install new apps and uninstall old ones. Just a few clicks to confirm the changes, and you're ready to enjoy the latest Vanilla OS experience.

While immutability protects the system, your data is a whole different story. That's why in Reunion we introduced Vanilla Continuity, a new snapshot-based backup and restore tool that is now part of the image and works together with ABRoot. It saves your home directories, the list of installed Flatpak apps and ABRoot metadata, then restores them when needed.

blocks.html_en: Vanilla uses a custom, graphical system installer. We are first asked to pick our preferred language from a list, then choose our keyboard from another list, and our timezone from a third list. We can then select which hard drive to use for storing Vanilla OS. The distribution offers guided partitioning which will take over an entire disk or manual partitioning. The manual option offers to launch the GParted application to help us organize the disk.

The manual option offers to launch the GParted application to help us organize the disk.

blocks.html_en: The installer offers to enable encryption on our partition and, if we accept, it will get us to make up a password to unlock the disk. The installer copies its files to the drive and then, in my case, it reported success. The system then reboots.

blocks.html_en: What I found intriguing, and sometimes frustrating, during my trial with Vanilla OS was that the distribution seems to be implementing some interesting concepts - even some complex and technically challenging concepts - and mostly doing it well, but none of it benefited me as a user. The distribution adds the complexity of immutability, but that's not helpful for me, that's something I need to work around. It's not as though the system being immutable is going to make the Debian base, of all things, more stable. Instead all it does is gum up the works when I try to run a terminal as the second user.

Since Vanilla isn't targeting beginners (their focus is on developer tools and containers) gearing their welcoming processes toward newcomers feels off brand.

blocks.html_en: Ultimately, Vanilla OS experiments with some technologies well, it makes running Debian with a layer of containers work (mostly) smoothly. As a proof of concept, it's a solid demonstration. Vanilla does a good job of layering tools like Flatpak on top of a Debian base. The question I kept asking myself throughout my trial though was: how does this help me use my computer? For me, the complexities added by Vanilla just impeded what I was doing, in ways Debian would not. Vanilla is heavier, it is more complex, it layers tools like Btrfs, zRAM, and Flatpaks which use up more resources. Vanilla sets up more mount points, runs more wizards, includes more container technology. All of this is interesting, but it doesn't make my computing experience or development processes faster or smoother or better in any practical way that I can find. Mostly, it made me want to switch to running the distribution's parent, Debian, to get the same underlying benefits without the extra layers and resource consumption.

blocks.html_en: Miscellaneous News (by Jesse Smith)

sentences.en: Miscellaneous News (by Jesse Smith)

blocks.html_en:
Asahi Linux works on M3-powered Apple computers, FreeBSD tests new service manager, Arch seeks help triaging bugs, openSUSE introduces tool to compare package versions, Linux Mint updates XApp, Debian publishes media update The Asahi Linux project has published good news for people running Apple's M-series hardware. The Asahi project now supports installing Linux on M3-powered devices: "It's been a while since we did a blog post outside of the progress reports, and today's as good an occasion for one as any; support for M3 series machines has now been merged into the installer. In other words, Asahi Linux now officially supports Macs with an M3 series SoC! Linux support for M3 series SoCs and the machines powered by them is now in a state where almost everything supported on the M1 and M2 series machines just works. This includes the webcam, internal microphones, USB (up to the hardware limit of USB 3 10Gb/s), hardware accelerated video decoding including support for AV1, WiFi, Bluetooth, and much more! The only major exceptions remain full DCP support and the GPU, which we will have more news on in the coming months. Do not expect performant or power-efficient 3D acceleration right now." Details on how to test M3 support, along with a list of limitations, are provided in the project's announcement.

* * * * *

Over the years there have been a number of discussions in the FreeBSD community regarding service management and possible alternatives to the current rc tools for launching services. Some alternatives have been tested over the years, including running OpenRC in the GhostBSD desktop offshoot of FreeBSD. Baptiste Daroussin has another option which is ready to test. The new tool, called rcd, imports a lot of the beneficial ideas from systemd while avoiding the pain points systemd has inflicted. "rcd(8) is a service manager daemon called by init(8) (in place of /etc/rc). It reads service definitions from UCL unit files (/etc/rcd.d/*.ucl), builds a dependency DAG, and starts services in parallel. After boot completes, it forks to background and stays running as a supervision daemon (automatically restarting failed services and accepting control commands via a UNIX socket)." The post from Daroussin goes on to share information on how to install and run rcd, list key features, and the message points out rcd is 100% compatible with the existing rc service manager, making switching between the two seamless.

* * * * *

Frederik Schwan of the Arch Linux project has put out a call for volunteers to help Arch deal with bug reports. Many projects have seen a surge in bug tickets in recent months, due to LLM-created reports, and Arch is hoping to get help triaging bugs submitted to their GitLab account. "We are searching for additional helping hands on our GitLab. Offering sources for thousands of packages requires triaging (and sometimes closing) the many issues that users report over time. As a bug wrangler you would be helping the distribution with triaging tickets across all package source repositories and assigning them to relevant package maintainers, as well as closing invalid ones and/or investigating the topics at hand (if applicable)." The post includes contact information where people can reach out to volunteer.

* * * * *

If you have ever wanted to compare the package versions between openSUSE's Leap and Tumbleweed branches and didn't want to manually compare the versions yourself, we have the DistroWatch package comparison page. This page will display the upstream stable version of a package as well as provide the package versions for any two distributions, or any two versions of a distribution. Now, alternatively, the openSUSE project provides its own implementation of this feature to compare packages between openSUSE Leap and openSUSE Tumbleweed. "The tool pulls the archive indexes straight from download.opensuse.org; this is for open-source software (oss) and non-oss, x86_64 and noarch and it's done for Tumbleweed, Leap 16.1, and Leap 16.0; then it compares the upstream version of every source package it finds. The result is a single sortable, filterable table with a timestamp on it." The new osdiff tool is now live and provides a filter for narrowing down the list of compared packages.

* * * * *

The Linux Mint project maintains a collection of applications, called XApp, which are desktop-neutral forks of GNOME applications. The XApps now have their own website to make it easier to discover and learn about the applications. "The XApp project started within Linux Mint but it has grown a lot since then. Its libraries, tools and applications are used in many desktops and distributions. It was given a new website to make it easier to discover all its components. Thingy, known as the 'Library' in the desktop, was redesigned. Until now, documents were grouped by application. For instance, PDF files and all the other document types supported by XReader were grouped together under 'Document Viewer'. The library now organizes documents by type instead. It no longer matters which applications are installed or which formats they support." Further information is provided in the Linux Mint monthly newsletter.

* * * * *

The Debian project has published updated install media for Debian 13 "Trixie". "The Debian project is pleased to announce the seventh update of its stable distribution Debian 13 (codename Trixie). This point release mainly adds corrections for security issues, along with a few adjustments for serious problems. Security advisories have already been published separately and are referenced where available. Please note that the point release does not constitute a new version of Debian 13 but only updates some of the packages included. There is no need to throw away old Trixie media. After installation, packages can be upgraded to the current versions using an up-to-date Debian mirror."

* * * * *

These and other news stories can be found on our Headlines page.

blocks.html_en: Questions and Answers (by Jesse Smith)

sentences.en: Questions and Answers (by Jesse Smith)

blocks.html_en:
The smallest possible Linux Honey-I-shrank-the-distro asks: Some people say Linux is smaller and lighter than other operating systems, but how small can Linux get compared to others?

DistroWatch answers: For the sake of comparison, Microsoft says the minimal system requirements for Windows 11 are: a dual-core, 64-bit x86_64 processor, 4GB of RAM, and 64GB of storage. Even the heavier Linux distributions require about half those resources to perform a full install and then run a desktop and a web browser.

Linux distributions can get really small! The smallest Linux distribution I've run on my own machines was about 1.4MB in size (that's megabytes, not gigabytes). It was called Tom's Root Boot and ran from a 3.5-inch floppy disk. It was quite minimal. It included the Linux kernel with minimal features enabled and a handful of command line tools only. It could be used for basic system rescue operations.

Granted, that was about 20 years ago and modern versions of the Linux kernel are a bit too big to run from a floppy disk. In recent memory, one of the smallest Linux distributions I have tried was Minimal Linux Live, which was about a 7MB download. That's just enough for the kernel, a shell, and a few userland utilities, again mostly for system rescue purposes.

There are a few other distributions which are in the same range. Tiny Core's most compact edition is about 17MB and SliTaz has an edition which is under 50MB.

These distributions are probably as small as you will be able to get, realistically, and still have an operating system which can boot on a personal computer. There are some smaller, embedded Linux distributions that are not meant for use by the general public. Linux can power all sorts of small devices and I've heard of people booting a Linux kernel on anything from home appliances to vape pens.

Whenever we talk about how small Linux can get or how few resources it can be made to consume, I think it is important to include context. Specifically, what do we want to accomplish with this miniature distribution? We can distill the Linux kernel and userland down to a few megabytes, but it won't be useful for many things. As soon as we start to add functionality, the size will need to creep upward. If we want a command line experience, we will need at least 10MB of disk space and around 25MB of RAM, if we want to add a graphical environment then the requirements go upward. Tiny Core Linux manages to provide a desktop and package manager with about 24MB of disk space and a little under 100MB of RAM. This is probably as small as we can get and provide any degree of practical personal computing.

In short, on the heavier end, big Linux distros can get by with about half the resources of Windows 11. On the lighter end, there are some Linux distributions which can run a small desktop and a few applications with about 1% of the resources Microsoft says Windows 11 requires.

* * * * *

Additional answers can be found in our Questions and Answers archive.

sentences.en: Released Last Week

blocks.html_en:
FreeBSD 14.5

The FreeBSD project has published an update to FreeBSD's 14.x series. The new version, 14.5, provides several fixes and introduces some changes to the userland utilities. "The rc.firewall script now supports reading IP addresses or subnets from on-disk files for the firewall_allowservices and firewall_trusted list variables. Elements that look like absolute paths are read line by line, skipping comments and blank lines, and the first word on each line is treated as an address or subnet. The default history size in sh(1) has been increased from 100 to 128, complying with the POSIX.1-2024 minimum requirement. LTO-10 and LTO-10P density codes and cartridge specifications have been added to mt(1) and libmt, enabling detection and reporting of the new tape formats. The default behaviour of pwd(1) has changed from -P to -L, aligning with POSIX semantics. The ipfw(8) binary now includes a fallback mechanism to support the new kernel interface introduced in FreeBSD 15.0. When running with a 15.0+ kernel, ipfw(8) automatically invokes a bundled ipfw15 binary to load firewall rules, ensuring compatibility during upgrade procedures. The daemon(8) utility now supports the -m option to specify the output file mode, allowing non-root log collectors to access log files." Additional information can be found in the release announcement and in the release notes.

Spaced Linux 9.26

Spaced Linux 9.26 has been released. Spaced Linux is a desktop Linux distribution based on Devuan's "Unstable" branch and featuring the MATE desktop environment with the Compiz compositing window manager. "Spaced Linux 9.26 is a major production release focused on upgrade reliability, graphics-driver recovery, desktop startup resilience, signed package delivery, and substantially stronger automated release validation. System updates and upgrade reliability: reworked Spaced Update to handle complete operating system upgrades more safely and predictably; added a dedicated APT transaction guard so package changes are protected during the actual locked package-management operation rather than only during preliminary checks; improved handling of package refreshes, native package upgrades, Flatpak updates, release-marker changes, and error reporting; added explicit testing for upgrades from earlier Spaced Linux installations to reduce the chance of regressions affecting existing users; added package-payload validation to confirm that the packages delivered by the production repository match the expected release; added release-identity checks so the built ISO, installed release metadata, package repository, and release version cannot silently drift apart...." Continue to the detailed release notes for further information.

Ubuntu 24.04.5

Utkarsh Gupta has announced an update to the Ubuntu 24.04 long-term support (LTS) branch of Canonical's operating system. The new update, version 24.04.5, introduces fixes and improvements: "Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, code-named 'Noble Numbat', is here. The team has been hard at work through this cycle, together with the community and our partners, to introduce new features and fix bugs. As usual, this point release includes many updates and updated installation media has been provided, so that fewer updates will need to be downloaded after installation. These include security updates and corrections for other high-severity bugs, with a focus on maintaining stability and compatibility with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS." The release announcement and release notes provide additional information for both Ubuntu and its community editions.

sentences.en: FreeBSD 14.5 The FreeBSD project has published an update to FreeBSD's 14.x series.
The new version, 14.5, provides several fixes and introduces some changes to the userland utilities.
"The rc.firewall script now supports reading IP addresses or subnets from on-disk files for the firewall_allowservices and firewall_trusted list variables.
Elements that look like absolute paths are read line by line, skipping comments and blank lines, and the first word on each line is treated as an address or subnet.
The default history size in sh(1) has been increased from 100 to 128, complying with the POSIX.1-2024 minimum requirement.
LTO-10 and LTO-10P density codes and cartridge specifications have been added to mt(1) and libmt, enabling detection and reporting of the new tape formats.
The default behaviour of pwd(1) has changed from -P to -L, aligning with POSIX semantics.
The ipfw(8) binary now includes a fallback mechanism to support the new kernel interface introduced in FreeBSD 15.0.
When running with a 15.0+ kernel, ipfw(8) automatically invokes a bundled ipfw15 binary to load firewall rules, ensuring compatibility during upgrade procedures.
The daemon(8) utility now supports the -m option to specify the output file mode, allowing non-root log collectors to access log files."
Additional information can be found in the release announcement and in the release notes.
Spaced Linux 9.26 Spaced Linux 9.26 has been released.
Spaced Linux is a desktop Linux distribution based on Devuan's "Unstable" branch and featuring the MATE desktop environment with the Compiz compositing window manager.

"Spaced Linux 9.26 is a major production release focused on upgrade reliability, graphics-driver recovery, desktop startup resilience, signed package delivery, and substantially stronger automated release validation.

System updates and upgrade reliability: reworked Spaced Update to handle complete operating system upgrades more safely and predictably; added a dedicated APT transaction guard so package changes are protected during the actual locked package-management operation rather than only during preliminary checks; improved handling of package refreshes, native package upgrades, Flatpak updates, release-marker changes, and error reporting; added explicit testing for upgrades from earlier Spaced Linux installations to reduce the chance of regressions affecting existing users; added package-payload validation to confirm that the packages delivered by the production repository match the expected release; added release-identity checks so the built ISO, installed release metadata, package repository, and release version cannot silently drift apart...."
Continue to the detailed release notes for further information.
